source.version_note: Published Frontiers in Psychology 9:1230, 18 July 2018; received 21 December 2017 and accepted 27 June 2018. The supplied ten-page article does not contain the separately referenced Appendix A.
source.verification_method: All ten supplied pages, footnotes and references read. Rendered pages 4, 6 and 7 visually checked against Tables 1–3; page 10 confirms the final references and declarations rather than an appendix. Publisher, PubMed and Crossref confirm identity/date. Public supplement identity and access were checked, but its DOCX content was not retrieved.

citation.title: Mind Perception of Robots Varies With Their Economic Versus Social Function

reading.source_scope_note: Four human rating studies concerning text-described robot roles and, in Study 2, robot images. Outcomes are attributed emotion/cognition and hypothetical willingness to sacrifice robots; there is no live robot interaction, actual injury, observed sentience or legal-rights determination.
access_limits: All ten main-article pages, three results tables, footnotes and bibliography read. The role-profile Appendix A is referenced but not part of this PDF.

Crossref component DOI 10.3389/fpsyg.2018.01230.s001 identifies Data_Sheet_1.docx. The publisher supplement URL redirects to the article with a filename but no usable asset link in inspected HTML; the search tool could not open the component URL.

PMC6058296 lists a public DOCX link, but downloading it returned an HTML preparing-to-download challenge rather than a ZIP/DOCX. No challenge was bypassed; the saved response was not counted as appendix content. The old and current-host OA service attempts returned 404.
No raw data, analysis code, preregistration or original instrument file was obtained. No cited book or empirical paper was independently fully read for this review, and no author was contacted.

study.samples: Study 1a: 151; Study 1b: 50; Study 2: 172; Study 3: 110, totaling 483 reported main-study participations. A separate role-value pilot has 56. Unique cross-study people and prior participation are not established.
study.roles: Social value means support and companionship; economic value means expected financial profits/corporate benefits. These operational descriptions do not define an entity’s intrinsic moral worth or human rights.
study.study_1a: Random three-group social/economic/no-role assignment, four profiles of the assigned role type per person, counterbalanced profile order. Emotion and cognition are separate three-item 0–100 composites. Role × mind-dimension interaction F(2,148)=4.44, p=.013. Emotion means social 25.9, economic 13.5, control 11.6; cognition 68.3/68.5/64.6 has no significant pair contrasts. Caregiver versus salesperson descriptions bundle relational and task information.
study.study_1b: Within-person role conditions with explicit financial versus social-value wording and shared basic profiles. Control always first; only social/economic order is counterbalanced. Role × mind-dimension F(2,98)=3.82, p=.025. Emotion 27.3/17.1/18.8; cognition 57.2/58.0/56.0. Control comparisons can include order effects.
study.study_2: Between-person social/economic role, within-person high/low/control value level, two three-item mind dimensions. Three neutral head-and-shoulder robot images with matching/background controlled and image-level assignments counterbalanced. Control always first, high/low randomized. Role × value-level × dimension F(2,340)=4.81, p=.009. Emotion interaction F(1.91,325)=5.19, p=.007; high social 36.9 exceeds control 24.7 and low social 26.9. Cognition interaction F(1.97,335)=4.13, p=.017; low economic 51.3 is below high 59.1 and control 60.1. These are actual formal interactions; fractional degrees of freedom are not automatically errors.
study.study_3: Within-person social/economic × high/low roles, four text descriptions in randomized order. Respondents imagine saving three robots from electromagnetic shock and rate willingness to sacrifice each, then expected pain/sadness. No robot is actually shocked and no single forced sacrifice or observed helping action occurs. Printed scale description says seven-point from 0 to 7; the original response format remains unknown.
study.study_3_results: Role × level multivariate interaction F(2,108)=22.3, p<.001, and harm interaction F(1,109)=6.97, p=.010 are reported. Emotion high/low social 3.62/2.43 and high/low economic 2.29/2.35. Harm willingness high/low social 2.95/5.56 and high/low economic 3.60/5.45. High social is lowest, but high economic value also lowers harm willingness relative to low economic value. The result is not exclusive protection from social value.
study.correlation: Reported r(440)=−.331 pools four ratings for each of 110 people. The main ANOVAs include repeated measures, but the correlation paragraph does not disclose a repeated-measures/cluster-aware estimator. It does not establish a causal path from attributed emotion to earlier harm ratings.
study.not_measured: Actual robot feelings, unconscious inference, default economic-role belief, real moral conduct, rights entitlement, longitudinal attachment, clinical benefit, trust and cooperation are not directly established. Discussion mentions some as interpretations or future research.

summary: Described social versus economic roles change attributed emotion/cognition in formally tested interactions. Preserve the role-to-trait inference concept and the measured hypothetical harm pattern, while bounding causal, psychometric and moral interpretations.

findings.definition: Inferring a person’s or agent’s dispositions or capacities from the social role it occupies.
findings.origin: Social psychology / social role theory / trait inference
findings.novelty_rationale: The direction is role information to attributed traits, distinct from predicting function from design, evaluating an agent–task match, or learning an interaction sequence. The source explicitly states this inferential process and tests robot-role effects on capacity ratings.

evidence.quote: People infer the traits of a target from his/her socially
can elicit different inferences of mental ability.

findings.evidence_scope: A named descriptive extraction from the paper’s social-role framework, supported by robot-role manipulations and real dimension/value interactions. Human judgments about described robots are measured; automaticity and actual robot traits are not.
findings.boundary: Roles can supply relevant evidence about training, duties or designed capabilities; inference is not inherently biased. Evaluate whether the attributed trait is supported rather than label every role-sensitive judgment an error. Gender categories do not establish inherent capacities, duties, rights or individual identity. Attributed emotion does not demonstrate machine sentience.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human role-to-capacity inference tested with robot descriptions/images; analogous model inference remains a proposal
findings.ai_proposal: Present otherwise matched agents with different role labels and test whether a model attributes unsupported personality, feeling or competence. Compare justified inferences from explicit qualifications with stereotype-driven additions, keeping legitimate role information and individual evidence distinct.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity the capacity for subjective feelings or sensations, such as pleasure, pain, fear or joy.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve role-sensitive human judgments within the existing construct, separating perceived capacity from demonstrated ability and hypothetical harm from actual treatment.

evidence.quote: experience emotions, have feelings, and be emotional

findings.evidence_scope: Studies 1a/1b/2 use three emotion items; social role and high social value increase ratings in specific contrasts with formally tested interactions. Study 3 instead asks expected pain and sadness after harm willingness.
findings.boundary: These are attributions, not actual feelings. Low overall emotion ratings and differing measures across studies limit claims of strong or universal sentience belief; Study 3 measures no cognition composite.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity a capacity for intentional thought, planning and action.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve role-sensitive human judgments within the existing construct, separating perceived capacity from demonstrated ability and hypothetical harm from actual treatment.
findings.evidence_scope: Study 2’s formal cognition role × value-level interaction includes lower ratings for low-economic-value robots. The operational composite concerns self-control, analytical thought and rationality rather than every aspect of agency.
findings.boundary: No significant cognition contrasts in Studies 1a/1b do not prove equality or complete independence from role. Study 2 supports a dimension-specific pattern, not a universal monotonic rule.

findings.definition: Ascribing or denying mental capacities to another entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve role-sensitive human judgments within the existing construct, separating perceived capacity from demonstrated ability and hypothetical harm from actual treatment.

evidence.quote: can elicit different inferences of mental ability.

findings.evidence_scope: The study distinguishes rated emotion/experience and cognition/agency and tests their differential sensitivity to role and value. It supplies another context for mind attribution, not proof that every person or culture has exactly two exhaustive mind dimensions.
findings.boundary: High composite reliability and a six-item pooled factor analysis do not establish a universal cognitive architecture, unconscious mechanism or genuine robot mind. Emotion/agency and warmth/competence remain related but distinct constructs.

findings.definition: Attributing to an entity a claim to moral consideration in how actions affect it.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve role-sensitive human judgments within the existing construct, separating perceived capacity from demonstrated ability and hypothetical harm from actual treatment.

evidence.quote: as eligible to deserve protection from harm.

findings.evidence_scope: The authors interpret Study 3 as moral patiency: high-social-value robots receive lower hypothetical harm willingness, with a formal role × level interaction. Emotion and harm ratings correlate, while economic value also affects harm willingness.
findings.boundary: The outcome is not a direct rights-entitlement item or actual injury/helping behavior. Emotion is asked after harm willingness and no mediation establishes causation. Legal rights, actual sentience, intrinsic worth and the proper moral rule do not follow from respondents’ ratings.

findings.definition: Judging how well an agent’s perceived capabilities match the demands of a particular task.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve role-sensitive human judgments within the existing construct, separating perceived capacity from demonstrated ability and hypothetical harm from actual treatment.

evidence.quote: Knowledge about the proposed function of a robot

findings.evidence_scope: Boundary clarification: this article changes proposed functions and then measures attributed capacities; it does not directly measure the appropriateness or matching of a perceived agent to a task.
findings.boundary: Do not merge role-to-trait inference with agent–task fit or count this as another empirical test of the existing task-fit measure.

source_corrections.correction: The point count and inclusive integer endpoints conflict. Preserve the printed 0–7 endpoints and mark the actual number/format of response options unresolved until the original instrument is available; do not invent a repaired scale.
source_corrections.scope: Confirmed internal descriptor inconsistency, not verified instrument reconstruction.

source_corrections.correction: Conventional power is 1−β; power .80 corresponds to β=.20. The prose likely uses β for power, but the original G*Power settings and intended analysis are not available. Treat reported sensitivity as author-reported, not preregistered sample planning or a demonstrated absence of low power.
source_corrections.scope: Notation correction with explicitly unresolved intended settings.

source_corrections.reported: High social value afforded rights as a moral patient; social value confers moral rights.
source_corrections.correction: Describe lower hypothetical willingness-to-sacrifice ratings for high-social-value profiles, with high economic value also reducing willingness relative to low economic value. This does not measure or establish actual rights, sentience, legal protection or a necessary exclusive emotion-to-rights causal mechanism.
source_corrections.scope: Inference boundary, not a correction of the reported significant interaction.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: The 440 rating pairs arise from 110 people × four roles. The paragraph does not specify a clustered/repeated-measures correlation. If r(440) denotes degrees of freedom, ordinary Pearson df would instead be 438; it may be an informal sample-count locator. Do not call it 440 independent people or assign an unverified estimator.

For 110 paired observations, t=7.01 corresponds to conventional dz≈.668, not the printed lower bound d≥1.34; 2t/√109≈1.343. Similarly t=2.87 gives dz≈.274 versus printed d≥.55. The pattern resembles an independent-groups conversion, but the authors do not define d and other paired standardizations exist. Record the ambiguity rather than silently replace authors’ d values.

Economic-role and no-role control nonsignificance does not establish that respondents defaulted to an economic-role belief. No direct default-belief or equivalence test is reported, and Studies 1b/2 fix control first.

Intuitive/subjective processing, biologically defined sentience, rights and future bonding are theoretical claims or interpretations. The experiment does not independently establish those propositions, and a robot’s role is not proof of its felt state.

The supplied main PDF ends with references and declarations. The separately identified public DOCX could not be retrieved as a document; exact full robot profiles and response-option interface remain unread/unverified.

methodological_limits: Convenience volunteers from London public areas and an online platform, predominantly young and described as predominantly Caucasian. No representative population or real-world robot-user prevalence estimate follows.
483 main-study participations plus a separate 56-person pilot are not verified as 539 unique people. Repeated role/image ratings are not new participants.

Formal interactions are present across all four studies and are preserved. Nonsignificant components do not establish equivalence, and different significant/null p-values alone are not the basis of this review’s interaction claims.

Study 1a bundles different job and relationship details. Study 1b gives explicit value descriptions; Study 2 counterbalances image assignment and standardizes the neutral presentation. Control always comes first in Studies 1b/2; active conditions are counterbalanced/randomized.

Composite reliability and limited PCA results concern the chosen items and samples, not a universal two-factor mind architecture or equivalence between emotion and warmth, or cognition and competence.

Study 3 is hypothetical, measures expected pain/sadness after sacrifice willingness, and provides no causal mediation or actual robot harm observation. Its pooled correlation requires repeated-data caution even though the main ANOVAs handle within-person factors.
Economic value also changes willingness to sacrifice. The study does not demonstrate that only social function can motivate protection, or that emotion ratings determine legitimate rights.

Response-scale notation, paired effect-size standardization and sensitivity-power notation have unresolved details; significant primary interactions are not discarded because of these secondary reporting problems.
No original data, code, preregistration, separate Appendix A or fully read cited-source/book was obtained. Bibliographic identity checks are not independent full-paper replications.

cross_paper_learning.finding: The mind-attribution literature supports varying structures and specific item facets. This paper’s two composites should not overwrite physiological, social-emotional or perceptual-cognitive facets as a universal model.

Perceived agent–task fit concerns matching task demands to perceived capabilities. Here assigned role information changes capacity judgments, a distinct inferential direction without a direct task-fit measure.
Ratings of patiency, self–other overlap and bargaining behavior differ. Here hypothetical willingness to sacrifice is narrower than moral rights or observed protective conduct.

Preserve actual formal moderator tests and measured outcomes while bounding mediator causality. Unlike a direct rights judgment or real donation, this article’s final outcome is hypothetical sacrifice willingness.

Selected robot descriptions and capacity scales require careful operational boundaries. Counterbalanced images help one confound but do not validate actual feelings, rights or a general causal mechanism.

deferred.term: Social versus economic function as two new behaviors
deferred.reason: These are manipulated role/value conditions, not two newly demonstrated psychological behaviors.

deferred.term: Objectification as a newly demonstrated mechanism
deferred.reason: Background discussion and an unread cited paper do not establish objectification in these participants or actual machine experience.
Inferred from a nonsignificant control comparison rather than directly measured; fixed control-first ordering also limits two studies.

deferred.term: Robot moral rights as an observed behavioral fact
deferred.reason: Rights language is the authors’ interpretation. The direct outcome is hypothetical harm willingness and no legal/sentience determination is tested.

limitations: One distinct process added; existing constructs enriched with explicit operational limits. Preserve eleven categories, stable detail IDs and unnumbered rows. No forced citation quota, invented annual counts, extra research page, full-paper Markdown copy or automatic ethical/harm edges.
